content: The cover design features a subtle, misty background image that symbolizes the well-documented health risks of smoke from combustible tobacco products and the less-studied emissions from electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), such as e-cigarettes. This imagery is intended to highlight the hazards associated with both traditional smoking and vaping. The full spectrum of health risks related to tobacco use extends beyond air contaminants. To emphasize the importance of a Tobacco-Free status (not just Smoke-Free) for workplaces and workers, the cover includes a text box. The NIOSH Current Intelligence Bulletin (CIB) 67, titled Promoting Health and Preventing Disease and Injury Through Workplace Tobacco Policies, disseminates new scientific information about occupational hazards. It builds on decades of public health efforts to reduce tobacco-related disease and death, marking 50 years since the first Surgeon General's report on the health consequences of smoking. Workers who use tobacco products or are employed in workplaces where smoking is permitted are exposed to carcinogenic and toxic components of tobacco and tobacco smoke. While cigarette smoking has declined, millions of workers still smoke, and smoking is still allowed in many workplaces. Other forms of tobacco, such as smokeless tobacco, also pose health risks to users. This bulletin addresses several aspects of tobacco use, including: Tobacco use among workers. Occupational health and safety concerns related to tobacco use. Existing regulations and recommendations limiting tobacco use in workplaces. Interventions to eliminate or reduce these hazards. Ideally, these policies should be paired with tobacco cessation support programs. Smoke-free zones should include all indoor areas, areas outside building entrances and air intakes, and all work vehicles. Employers should also comply with OSHA and MSHA regulations prohibiting smoking in areas with explosive, flammable, or toxic materials. Tobacco use is a leading cause of debilitating and fatal diseases, including cancer, respiratory diseases, and cardiovascular diseases. These conditions primarily affect users but also occur in those exposed to SHS. Smoking is particularly hazardous, but smokeless tobacco also causes adverse health effects. More than 16 million U.S. Tobacco use in workplaces can amplify the risks of occupational hazards. Comprehensive workplace cessation programs that integrate tobacco cessation support into broader health and safety initiatives are particularly effective. Tobacco use continues to cause substantial health and economic burdens. Employers are encouraged to adopt comprehensive tobacco-free workplace policies and support cessation efforts to protect worker health and well-being.
